accuracy.evidence: Checked the age expectations against Development Matters 2021: 3 to 4 'tell a long story' and 'use a wider range of vocabulary', Reception 'retell the story' and 'describe events in some detail', and Literacy 'anticipate key events in stories'. Sequence words first, next, then and last are used as connectives the way the DfE Year 1 English programme describes; next and then are both accepted for middle cards rather than forcing one 'right' word, which would be a false rule.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-sequencing slips: putting the most exciting picture first (Mo, m5), believing any order tells the same story (swap prediction, challenge 'same'), using last for the middle or first at the end (tell scene feedback, challenge 'end'/'mid'), and repeating an earlier event as the ending (ending scene 'again'). Naming pictures instead of saying what happens is named in the adult text and modelled by the telling captions.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagpicstory is built around narrative: the canvas reads the story back in the learner's current order, so a swap of the egg cards literally narrates 'a chick, then it cracks, then an egg', and the ending scene asks for a consequence of earlier cards. It is not flagorder (time words for a seed and a day) or flagrefrain; the gate measured its source under 30% similar to every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Wrong placements in the balloon story are refused with the reason ('Ben needs the balloon before the wind can blow it'), so the child discovers the before-this question; the swap scene lets them hear the silly story themselves before the text says order matters; fixing three stories requires finding the card that cannot happen yet; the ending scene ties the last card to what came before.

predictions.evidence: Swap prediction offers 'same pictures, same story', which young children often believe, and the narrated swapped story disproves it. Spot-the-mix-up prediction offers 'any order is fine' for shoes before socks, which the scene then refuses with 'Socks go on before shoes'.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six why() messages, each naming the slip: chick before the egg cracks (swap), a swap changes the story (same), last used at the start (end), then used at the start (mid), an ending that repeats the start (again), and an ending from outside the story (off).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use one idea per short sentence with words a 3 to 4 year old hears daily (cards, story, start, end, swap, silly); canvas captions are 2 to 4 words ('It rains', 'Bake it'). validate_lessons.py readability passed; adult text stays under the 9.5 limit.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph carries one step: cards tell a story, the four sequence words, order matters (egg and chick), and the before-this question. Adult paragraphs cover curriculum, how to run it at home, named mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with other lessons.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots in light and dark after Show me and mid-demo: three-card rows are about 100 px wide and four-card rows about 80 px, captions wrap to at most three lines inside the card, First/Next/Then/Last labels sit under each card, and the dashed empty slots and the ? box are clearly visible in both themes. Full-width buttons under the canvas repeat every move.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas move has a button: put a card in the next place, say a word for the next card, swap card 1 and 2 / 2 and 3 / 1 and 3, tap each card in the mix-up story, and choose each ending. Each action updates the canvas aria-label and the live region, including the full story read back in order. walk.cjs ran axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) on desktop and iPhone 13 in both themes with no violations; canvas text is dark ink on white or pale cards.
